title: I believe
hookLine: a creed from credo, I believe: a short summary said together for centuries

lines: I BELIEVE. I BELIEVE. I BELIEVE.
cards: Rome, around the year 200, as an early church handbook describes it. It's the night before Easter, and a woman stands waist-deep in water, about to be baptized. She's spent months, maybe years, learning.
Now the bishop asks her three questions. Do you believe in God the Father Almighty? I believe, she says, and she goes under the water.
Do you believe in Christ Jesus, the Son of God? I believe, and under again. Do you believe in the Holy Spirit, and the holy church?
I believe. A third time. She comes up dripping, into a new life.

teach.h: CREDO: TO SET YOUR HEART ON.
teach.b: Creed comes from the Latin credo, I believe, the creed's first word. Some language historians link credo to an old phrase meaning to put your heart on something.
So believing isn't only agreeing with an idea; it's setting your heart on someone. In the West, the shorter creed is the Apostles' Creed.
A lovely old legend says the twelve apostles each wrote one line of it, on the day of Pentecost. It isn't true; historians trace it to those baptism questions in Rome, slowly shaped over centuries.
But it does carry the apostles' faith. In the English of the old prayer book it begins: "I believe in God the Father Almighty, Maker of heaven and earth."

Then Jesus: born, suffered, crucified, died, buried, descended, rose, ascended, and coming again. Then the Holy Spirit, the church, the communion of saints, forgiveness, the resurrection of the body, the life everlasting.

teach.h: A SYMBOL: A TOKEN BROKEN IN TWO.
teach.b: Early Christians called a creed a symbol, from the Greek symbolon, a token broken in two, whose halves fit together to prove who you were.

teach.h: LINE BY LINE, FOR TWO WEEKS.
teach.b: Say the creed, and you show which family you belong to.

teach.h: I BELIEVE IN GOD THE FATHER ALMIGHTY.
teach.b: Not every Christian uses creeds: Quakers keep no set creed, and some Baptists and Churches of Christ say they have no creed but the Bible, while holding much of the same faith.
For two weeks, the path walks the creed one phrase a day, starting tomorrow with what it says first about God.

how: Many churches say the Apostles' Creed at baptisms and at morning and evening prayer, and the Nicene Creed at the main Sunday service, with the whole congregation speaking together.

games.q: Rome, around the year 200. you're waist-deep in water, about to be baptized. the bishop asks: do you believe in God the Father Almighty? what happens next?
o: you say I believe, and go under the water.
games.why: early baptisms asked three questions. each time: I believe, and under the water. those questions grew into the creed.

practice: Rest a hand on your chest, where the old phrase put belief, and say quietly: I believe. Notice how it sounds in your own voice, and what comes to mind.
If you pray, go on with the creed's first line, I believe in God the Father Almighty, Maker of heaven and earth; if you don't, let the two words rest under your hand.
